# Diagnosing a Water-Induced Chrysler 300C No-Start Condition

Driving through a deep puddle and suddenly losing the ability to crank the engine is a classic symptom of electrical intrusion, but it rarely happens overnight. In your specific case, the vehicle started for a few seconds three times before stalling permanently. This behavior indicates that the battery holds a charge and the starter motor can engage, yet the ignition system or fuel delivery is failing immediately after the initial spark. The fact that the car worked fine initially and then failed after waiting a couple of hours suggests a thermal expansion issue or water sitting in a critical low point, rather than an immediate short circuit that would have killed power instantly.

The most likely culprit is water ingress into the ignition coil pack or the crankshaft/camshaft position sensors located near the bottom of the engine bay. The Chrysler 300C utilizes a timing chain drive with these sensors positioned on the lower intake manifold area, which is exactly where splash from high water accumulates. When you drove through the puddle, water likely bypassed the splash shields or entered through rubber boots. While the engine was running, the coolant and oil temperatures were elevated, allowing the metal components to expand and temporarily push the moisture away from the sensor contacts. Once the engine cooled down over those couple of hours, the components contracted, and the pooled water bridged the electrical contacts again, cutting off the signal required for the Engine Control Module (ECM) to time the spark.

To diagnose this systematically, you need to check the crankshaft position sensor first. This is a Hall-effect or magnetic pickup style sensor that sits very low on the engine block. If water has pooled around its connector or the wire insulation is compromised, moisture can travel down the harness. You should inspect the connector for green oxidation or bent pins. A common pitfall is assuming the sensor itself is dead; often, it is simply wet. Cleaning the connector with electrical contact cleaner and applying dielectric grease to the inside of the boot can prevent future recurrence. Dielectric grease acts as a hydrophobic barrier that prevents water from adhering to the metal contacts while remaining non-conductive.

Another possibility involves the ignition coil packs. On many 300C models, these coils are mounted on top of the cylinder heads. While less likely to be flooded directly by wheel splash unless the puddle was extremely deep, water can travel along the wiring harness. If the coils are failing intermittently, the ECM might not register a valid spark event and will cut power after a few seconds to protect itself. Use an OBD-II scanner to check for codes P0335 (Crankshaft Position Sensor "A" Circuit) or random misfire codes like P0300. These codes confirm whether the sensor is sending erratic data due to moisture.

If the sensors are clean and dry after cleaning, you must consider the starter solenoid. Water can cause the internal contacts of the solenoid to corrode or short internally, leading to a failure that only manifests under specific thermal conditions. However, given the "no crank" symptom appearing after cooling, the sensor path remains the primary suspect.

There is also a critical consideration regarding the battery terminals and ground straps. If the chassis ground strap was exposed to water, corrosion could form rapidly as the moisture evaporates from the metal surfaces. Ensure the negative battery terminal is tight and free of white or green corrosion. A poor ground can mimic a sensor failure by preventing the ECM from completing its circuit for ignition.

If cleaning and reseating connections does not resolve the issue, the wiring harness insulation may have been melted or cracked by the water's heat or impact. In such cases, repairing the harness with high-quality heat-shrink tubing containing adhesive liner is superior to simple electrical tape, which can fail under vibration and moisture. Always verify that any repair maintains the original wire gauge and routing to avoid chafing against other components during future driving cycles.
